topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focused on European public health context; competency frameworks may require adaptation for Australian healthcare systems, regulatory environments, and workforce structures.
takeaways: Review identifies core digital competencies needed in public health roles; consider which competencies are most critical for your organisation's AI upskilling priorities and how they map to existing job descriptions.

European framework may highlight gaps between current workforce capability and future digital public health needs; use it as a benchmark to assess your team's current AI literacy baseline and identify targeted training areas.

Competency frameworks from this review could inform curriculum design for internal AI capability development programs, though Australian public health policy and workplace contexts will require contextualisation.

articles.title: Developing a competency framework for artificial intelligence in undergraduate dental education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Developing a competency framework for artificial intelligence in undergraduate dental education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on dental education specifically. Framework may have limited direct applicability to non-healthcare sectors or general AI literacy programs, though competency-building principles could transfer.
takeaways: Competency frameworks for AI should be tailored to profession-specific contexts (e.g., how dentists use AI diagnostically) rather than generic literacy approaches — this model could inform similar frameworks in other regulated professions.
Undergraduate education is a critical entry point for AI capability development; integrating AI competencies early prevents capability gaps and sets professional practice standards.
Structured competency frameworks clarify expected learning outcomes and assessment criteria, making AI training measurable and scalable across educational institutions.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited by focus on middle school education context; unclear whether findings and frameworks apply to adult workplace learning or other educational levels. Geographic scope not specified in snippet.
takeaways: Consider how AI literacy can be embedded within broader digital competency frameworks rather than taught in isolation — this holistic approach may improve transfer to real-world application.
Middle school frameworks may offer insights into foundational AI concepts and mental models that could inform how you scaffold AI learning for employees with limited prior exposure.

articles.title: The application of artificial intelligence in the context of person-centred care – a discourse on pitfalls and possibilities - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The application of artificial intelligence in the context of person-centred care – a discourse on pitfalls and possibilities  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — a conceptual discourse on AI and person-centred care that likely draws on global literature, but without explicit geographic scope or empirical data, applicability may vary by healthcare system and context.
takeaways: Understand key pitfalls of AI implementation in person-centred care (e.g. algorithmic bias, loss of human judgment, patient autonomy concerns) before deploying AI tools in your organisation.

Design AI literacy programmes that address both technical capability and ethical reasoning — staff need to understand not just how to use AI, but when and why human-centred judgment should override algorithmic recommendations.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG analysis draws on global consulting experience but findings are most directly applicable to large, well-resourced organisations. Specific implementation context and geographic regulatory requirements not detailed in snippet.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption internally as a people-centric change initiative, not just a technology rollout — workforce readiness and capability building must be planned alongside technical implementation.
Audit current skill gaps and design targeted upskilling programs before deploying AI tools, rather than expecting staff to learn on the job.
Establish clear role transitions and career pathways for employees whose work will change due to AI, to manage retention and engagement during transformation.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to focus on public health faculty development context; applicability to other sectors and geographic regions unclear without full article details.
takeaways: Faculty resistance to AI adoption is addressable through structured development programs; design interventions that move educators from skepticism to confidence rather than assuming buy-in.

AI literacy initiatives in educational settings require instructor capability-building as a prerequisite; investing in faculty development yields better cascading outcomes for student learning than top-down policy alone.
Public health educators uniquely positioned to embed AI literacy into workforce preparation; consider what sector-specific AI literacy competencies matter most before designing generic training.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Cannot assess from title and snippet alone — methodology and sample details are needed to determine geographic scope and applicability to Australian organisational contexts.
takeaways: Role ambiguity (unclear expectations about how to use AI) and self-efficacy (confidence in your ability to use AI effectively) are two distinct factors affecting employee-AI collaboration — addressing both through clear role definition and targeted capability-building is more effective than focusing on one alone.

When introducing AI tools, clarify how the technology fits into employees' existing roles and responsibilities, and provide scaffolded training to build confidence — these two interventions work through different psychological pathways to improve adoption.

articles.title: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study - Nature
articles.snippet: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — findings are based on nurses' experiences with medical AI and may not generalise to other healthcare roles or non-healthcare sectors. Three-wave design strengthens causal inference but sample size and geographic scope are unclear from the snippet.
takeaways: Work autonomy is a critical lever: ensure staff retain meaningful control over decisions when implementing medical AI, rather than positioning AI as a replacement for human judgment — this directly protects wellbeing outcomes.
AI readiness alone isn't enough for positive outcomes — pair technical training and capability-building with explicit organisational commitment to preserving staff autonomy and agency in workflows.
When rolling out medical AI, assess and strengthen autonomy first: staff who feel they control how and when AI is used experience better psychological wellbeing, even when AI adoption is required.

articles.title: How AI is reshaping human skills and thinking - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: How AI is reshaping human skills and thinking  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a position piece or editorial from the APA rather than empirical research. Likely focuses on US psychological context but may include broader conceptual frameworks applicable to understanding AI's impact on cognition and skill development.
takeaways: Consider how AI tools may be changing not just what skills employees need, but how they think and process information — this warrants ongoing assessment in your workforce development strategy.
Use this as a prompt to evaluate whether your organisation's AI training programmes address both technical competence and the cognitive adaptations required to work effectively alongside AI systems.

articles.title: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on the study's sample composition and methodology, which are not evident from the title and snippet alone. The theoretical framework (Automation–Augmentation Paradox) is conceptually transferable across contexts, but empirical applicability would depend on sector, organisation type, and employee roles studied.
takeaways: Generative AI adoption creates a dual effect on employee knowledge work: automation can reduce knowledge-sharing behaviours while augmentation may enhance skill development—organisations need to actively design processes that encourage knowledge collaboration rather than assuming AI adoption alone will improve knowledge behaviours.

When implementing generative AI, explicitly address the 'augmentation' pathway by defining roles where AI amplifies rather than replaces employee expertise, paired with training that frames AI as a knowledge-enhancing tool to counteract deskilling risk.

articles.title: Employees Are Relying on AI for Personal Support. That’s Risky. - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Employees Are Relying on AI for Personal Support. That’s Risky.  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Moderate — presents general principles about employee AI use and organisational risk, but lacks empirical evidence or specific data on prevalence, sectors, or geographies. Applicability depends on your organisation's AI adoption context.
takeaways: Establish clear organisational policies on which AI tools employees can use for work and personal matters during work hours, specifying data privacy, confidentiality, and security requirements.
Provide training to help employees understand the risks of sharing sensitive personal or professional information with consumer AI tools (e.g. data retention, third-party use, model training).
Create accessible alternative support resources (mentoring, counselling, professional development) so employees don't default to AI for guidance on career, wellbeing, or decision-making issues.

articles.title: Human-computer interaction: catalyst or drain? Dual pathways of employee creativity from a psychological resources perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Human-computer interaction: catalyst or drain? Dual pathways of employee creativity from a psychological resources perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unable to assess without full article access — generalisability depends on sample size, sector diversity, and geographic scope, which are not evident from title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Employee creativity with AI tools follows two distinct pathways: some employees experience enhanced psychological resources and creativity gains, while others experience resource depletion — assess which pathway your team members are on to tailor support accordingly.

Psychological resources (e.g., cognitive capacity, emotional resilience, motivation) mediate the relationship between human-computer interaction and creative output — monitor these resources and provide targeted interventions (workload management, training, psychological safety) to shift employees from the 'drain' to 'catalyst' pathway.

Not all AI adoption automatically boosts creativity; the impact depends on how interaction with technology affects individual psychological states — design implementation strategies that protect and replenish psychological resources rather than assuming technology adoption alone will drive creative gains.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte's framework is based on consulting experience across multiple sectors, but without disclosed sample details, generalisability to specific organisational contexts is unclear. Likely most applicable to large enterprises with resources for structured change management.
takeaways: Shift from 'AI adoption' (tool implementation) to 'AI adaptation' (behaviour change) — success depends on embedding new ways of working and thinking, not just deploying technology.

Design change interventions that target human behaviours explicitly: identify which roles need which capabilities, then sequence training and support to build those behaviours incrementally rather than expecting overnight transformation.

Create feedback loops and reinforcement mechanisms during the adaptation phase — monitor adoption metrics, celebrate early wins, and course-correct based on where people are struggling with new AI-enabled workflows.

articles.title: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective - Nature
articles.snippet: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on the study's sample composition and geographic scope, which are not detailed in the snippet. The theoretical framework (cognitive appraisal and Job Demands-Resources) is widely applicable, but findings may vary across different organisational contexts, industries, and cultural settings.
takeaways: Employee awareness of AI can trigger job crafting through two distinct pathways — one involving stress appraisal and another leveraging job resources — suggesting tailored interventions should address both emotional and structural dimensions rather than a one-size-fits-all approach.

Understanding how employees cognitively appraise AI-related stress is critical for designing change initiatives; framing AI as a tool that augments rather than replaces roles may shift appraisals from threat to opportunity, enabling proactive job crafting.

Organisations should assess and enhance job resources (autonomy, support, skill development) as a parallel strategy to change awareness, since the JD-R pathway suggests employees are more likely to craft jobs positively when they perceive adequate resources to manage AI integration.

articles.title: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey analysis typically draws on client work across geographies and sectors, but specific case details and applicability to smaller organisations or non-consulting contexts may be limited.
takeaways: Map your organisation's AI transformation across three distinct phases (adoption, scaling, impact) to identify which stage you're in and what capabilities need development next, rather than treating AI implementation as a single event.

Use the 'three horizons' framework to balance immediate AI literacy needs (horizon 1) with medium-term capability building (horizon 2) and long-term strategic impact (horizon 3) — helps prioritise training and behaviour change efforts.

Recognise that moving from AI adoption to measurable business impact requires sustained behaviour change; identify specific behaviours and processes that need to shift at each horizon to embed AI effectively into workflows.

articles.title: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford GSB perspective piece without specified empirical research base, geographic scope, or industry sampling. Findings may reflect US higher education and business school viewpoints.
takeaways: Identify specific work processes in your organisation where AI adoption could require behaviour change, then map the skill gaps and mindset shifts needed before implementation.
Use this as a starting point to design targeted upskilling or change management interventions, but supplement with local data about your workforce's readiness and concerns around AI adoption.

articles.title: AI-induced job crafting: a systematic review of cognitive appraisal pathways - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI-induced job crafting: a systematic review of cognitive appraisal pathways  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — systematic reviews synthesise existing research but generalisability depends on the quality and geographic diversity of included studies, which is not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Job crafting—proactively redesigning tasks and roles in response to AI—is mediated by how employees cognitively interpret AI's impact (threat vs. opportunity); understanding these appraisal pathways helps organisations design interventions that shift negative threat perceptions toward adaptive reframing.

Organisations can support AI-induced job crafting by explicitly facilitating cognitive reappraisal opportunities (e.g., training, dialogue, role redesign workshops) rather than assuming employees will naturally adapt their jobs to complement new technology.

Individual differences in cognitive appraisal styles affect how readily employees craft their roles; tailored change strategies that account for these differences (e.g., cognitive flexibility, prior tech experience) are likely more effective than one-size-fits-all upskilling programmes.

articles.title: Challenge or threat? The double-edged sword effect of AI use on innovative teaching behavior among primary and secondary school teachers in China | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: Challenge or threat? The double-edged sword effect of AI use on innovative teaching behavior among primary and secondary school teachers in China | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited to Chinese educational context — findings on teacher responses to AI may not generalise to Australian schools due to differences in institutional support, digital infrastructure, teacher training systems, and cultural attitudes toward technology adoption.
takeaways: AI implementation in schools can have paradoxical effects: while it creates opportunities for innovation, it simultaneously triggers threat responses that inhibit risk-taking — monitor teacher stress and engagement levels during rollout, not just adoption rates.

The 'double-edged sword' dynamic suggests that technical enablement alone is insufficient; design change initiatives to actively address teacher anxiety about AI competence and job security to unlock the innovative potential.

Apply a contingency approach: tailor your AI literacy programme based on whether teachers frame AI as a challenge (opportunity for growth) or threat (risk) — those viewing it as threat need different support, messaging, and psychological safety scaffolding.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism - PsyPost
articles.snippet: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — appears to report on recent psychology research but geographic scope and sample characteristics are not described.
takeaways: Antagonistic narcissism (dominance-seeking, hostility) paradoxically attracts some romantic partners in the short term, possibly because assertiveness reads as confidence and charisma.

The finding is counterintuitive because we expect narcissistic traits to repel; the research suggests narcissists' boldness and self-assuredness can be mistaken for desirable leadership qualities in early attraction.
This highlights why people sometimes pursue relationships with 'bad' partners — narcissistic charm is real and compelling, even though long-term outcomes are typically poor.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear from snippet alone — likely limited to laboratory conditions and specific personality measures tested, with unclear geographic scope.
takeaways: Surprise acts as a powerful memory amplifier, but its effect varies dramatically depending on personality type — some people genuinely remember unexpected moments better than others, while for some the boost is minimal.

This research suggests your personality might predispose you to be either a 'surprise rememberer' or someone who processes shocking moments more evenly with routine ones — a counterintuitive twist on the common assumption that everyone remembers surprises equally well.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - ScienceDaily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  ScienceDaily
articles.generalisability: Limited — headline-driven summary of research without details on sample size, methodology, or study population; the underlying research may have limited generalisability depending on original study design.
takeaways: Brain imaging studies have identified structural or functional differences in people with psychopathic traits, though what counts as 'shocking' often depends on media framing rather than the magnitude of the actual effect.

Neuroscientific findings about psychopathy are fascinating because they challenge the idea that antisocial behaviour is purely a choice — yet brain differences don't determine destiny, and most people with similar brain patterns aren't criminals.
The gap between 'we found a brain difference' and 'we can now predict or treat psychopathy' remains huge; neuroimaging is excellent at group-level patterns but poor at individual prediction.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — scope and sample size not specified. Findings may be limited to English-language wine reviews and may not generalise across cultures with different wine-drinking traditions or review practices.
takeaways: An AI system detected meaningful personality signals in how people write about wine — suggesting our word choices reveal consistent patterns about who we are, even in seemingly mundane consumer reviews.

Wine review language contains enough personality signal that machines can pick it up, which is counterintuitive since most people don't think they're revealing personality when describing a Pinot Noir.
This hints at a fun party trick: the way someone describes a bottle might say more about them than about the wine itself.

articles.title: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs - PsyPost
articles.snippet: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on twin study sample size and composition, which is not detailed in the snippet. Twin studies typically use Western, educated samples and may not reflect authoritarian belief patterns globally.
takeaways: Twin studies can tease apart nature vs. nurture in political attitudes — authoritarian beliefs appear to have a heritable component that researchers didn't expect.
The finding is counterintuitive because people usually assume political ideology is purely learned from family environment and culture, not baked into temperament or genetics.
This touches on a deeper puzzle: if authoritarian beliefs are partly genetic, what exactly is being inherited — personality traits, cognitive style, or something else?

articles.title: Your personality may be more genetic than scientists realized - ScienceDaily
articles.snippet: Your personality may be more genetic than scientists realized  ScienceDaily
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — appears to summarize research findings but lacks detail on sample scope, methodology, or original study location.
takeaways: Personality traits may have a stronger hereditary component than previous estimates suggested, challenging the nature-nurture balance assumptions many people hold.

This finding is counterintuitive because it suggests environmental factors matter less for shaping core personality than commonly believed — raising interesting questions about how much personal effort actually changes who we are.
If personality is more 'baked in' genetically, it reframes how we think about self-improvement, compatibility in relationships, and whether people can truly reinvent themselves.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: When inclusive leadership promotes innovation: the role of team psychological safety and leader power distance orientation - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When inclusive leadership promotes innovation: the role of team psychological safety and leader power distance orientation  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample composition — without access to the full article, the scope is unclear, but findings on psychological safety and inclusive leadership likely apply broadly across sectors where innovation is valued, though cultural context (power distance orientation) may moderate effects.
takeaways: Inclusive leadership strengthens the link between psychological safety and team innovation — ensure your leadership approach explicitly invites diverse perspectives and ideas, not just permits them.

A leader's orientation toward power distance (hierarchical vs. egalitarian) shapes how psychological safety translates to innovation outcomes — reflect on whether your team perceives you as approachable and willing to challenge hierarchy, or as maintaining formal distance.

Psychological safety alone is insufficient for innovation; it must be paired with inclusive leadership behaviours (e.g., soliciting input, acknowledging diverse viewpoints, admitting uncertainty) to realise its benefit.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025  PwC
articles.generalisability: Broad — PwC's survey typically covers large multi-country samples across diverse sectors and employment levels, though specific sample composition and weighting methods are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Identify the specific psychological safety concerns and fears emerging in your workforce by comparing results to your own employee sentiment data — this can help prioritise interventions where safety gaps are most acute.

Use workforce hopes data to understand what conditions employees believe would enable them to perform better and feel safer, then map these to concrete policy or cultural changes you can pilot in your organisation.
Monitor how psychological safety concerns vary by geography and sector in the survey — this can inform whether your safety initiatives need localised or role-specific tailoring.

articles.title: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams  Frontiers
articles.sample: Academic teams — geographic scope not specified from title/snippet
articles.generalisability: Limited — findings from academic settings may not generalise to corporate or other organisational contexts. Sample characteristics, team size, and AI tool specifications unknown from snippet provided.
takeaways: AI tools can be designed to prompt leaders toward more inclusive behaviours; explore whether your organisation's leadership systems or decision-support tools include similar nudges for inclusive team dynamics.

Gendered outcomes in multicultural teams may be measurable and addressable through structured leadership practices — consider auditing whether your team composition, speaking time, or project allocation shows patterns by gender or cultural background.

AI-assisted interventions work best when paired with psychological safety; ensure any new tool or process doesn't create the appearance of 'outsourced' fairness, which could undermine trust in human leadership.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on the study's sample composition, which is not detailed in the snippet provided. The mechanism linking AI adoption to depression through psychological safety erosion may apply broadly, but sector, organisational context, and geographic scope would affect applicability.
takeaways: Monitor and protect psychological safety explicitly during AI implementation — the erosion of trust and safety may be a hidden pathway to employee wellbeing harm that leaders overlook.

Ethical leadership is protective: organisations adopting AI should prioritise transparent communication about change, involve employees in implementation decisions, and model ethical use of AI systems to maintain psychological safety.

Screen for depression and mental health impacts post-AI adoption, particularly among employees who experience reduced autonomy or increased surveillance — this may be an underrecognised occupational health risk.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG's findings likely draw from their consulting work across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific sample composition and methodology are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Create explicit norms that invite diverse voices and perspectives in meetings and decision-making to reduce status-based barriers and ensure all employees feel their input is valued.
Assess current psychological safety levels in your team through anonymous surveys or listening sessions, then address identified gaps through manager coaching on creating safe speaking environments.

Design feedback and innovation processes that actively solicit contributions from quieter or lower-status employees, signalling that psychological safety applies equally across all hierarchical levels.

articles.title: Human capabilities are at the heart of high-performing teams - Deloitte
articles.snippet: Human capabilities are at the heart of high-performing teams  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Limited — Deloitte practitioner report with no disclosed sample size, methodology, or geographic scope. Findings likely reflect Deloitte's client base (predominantly large organisations) and may not generalise to small-to-medium enterprises or non-client contexts.
takeaways: Identify which human capabilities (communication, trust, collaboration, emotional intelligence) are currently underdeveloped in your teams, then design targeted interventions — psychological safety depends on team members feeling confident enough to speak up, which requires explicit skill-building, not assumption.

Create mechanisms to measure psychological safety in your team (e.g. pulse surveys on speaking up, asking for help, admitting mistakes) before and after capability-building initiatives to track whether investment in human capability translates to safer team dynamics.
